Tan Family Register and Genealogical Notes
Family register and genealogical notes

---

1. Tan Ah Kow (頭家, "Towkay" Tan)
Birth: 15 March 1810 (recorded in the hand of his father, Tan Seng Huat, on the day of the birth; the entry is in ink and remains the authoritative record for all later family histories).

The entry reads: "On this fifteenth day of the third month, in the year of our Lord eighteen hundred and ten, was born to me, Tan Seng Huat, and my wife Lim Neo, a son. He is the firstborn. We name him Ah Kow. May he grow strong and bring honour to the family. This I write with my own hand, at Malacca."

Marginal note, added by Tan Ah Kow's eldest grandson, Tan Boon Keng, in 1895: "This is the date of the Towkay's birth. All other dates given for him in later papers are mistaken. He was born in Malacca, not in Penang as some say. He came to Singapore in 1828."

A second marginal note, in pencil, by an unknown hand, likely in the 1930s: "The old Towkay's birth date is sometimes given as 1810-03-15. This is the correct one, as per this register."

2. Tan Seng Huat (father of Tan Ah Kow)
Birth: circa 1775, in Malacca. The exact day is not recorded. He was the son of Tan Cheng Kee, a trader in spices and cloth.
Death: 12 June 1835, at Malacca. The entry is in the hand of Tan Ah Kow, who was present at the deathbed. The cause is noted as "a long illness of the chest."

3. Lim Neo (mother of Tan Ah Kow, née Lim)
Birth: circa 1778, in Malacca. Her family were farmers in the hinterland.
Death: 3 January 1840, at Singapore, in the house of her son. The entry notes: "She had come to live with her son in the new settlement, and was happy to see her grandchildren. She died in her sleep, at the age of about sixty-two."

In the family register, Tan Ah Kow's birth_date is noted as 1810-03-15. Record status: historical.

4. Tan Ah Kow's Siblings
The register lists the following brothers and sisters, all born in Malacca. The dates for the younger children are less precise, as they were recorded from memory by the mother.

- Tan Ah Lian (sister), born circa 1812. Married a trader from Penang, one Khoo Cheng Teik, in 1830. She moved to Penang and had three children. The register notes: "She is well, and writes to us sometimes." No death date is recorded in this volume.
- Tan Ah Chye (brother), born circa 1814. Died in infancy, in 1815, of fever. The entry is terse: "The child did not live to see his second year."
- Tan Ah Seng (brother), born 1817, on a date not specified. He became a planter in Province Wellesley. Married in 1843 to a woman named Goh Kim Neo. The register records the marriage but gives no further details. He is mentioned in later entries as a correspondent.
- Tan Ah Neo (sister), born circa 1820. She remained unmarried and lived with the family until her death in 1862, which is recorded in a later volume.

5. Notes on Tan Ah Kow's Marriage
Tan Ah Kow married Lim Guat Neo, daughter of Lim Peng Soon, a Malacca merchant, in 1832. The entry is in the hand of the bride's father, who wrote: "On the twentieth day of the sixth month, I gave my daughter to Tan Ah Kow, a young man of good character and prospects. The ceremony was held at my house in Malacca. May they be blessed with many sons."

Marginal note by Tan Ah Kow's grandson: "The Towkay's wife was known as 'Bibik Guat'. She was a strong woman, and managed the household while he built his business."

6. Tan Ah Kow's Children (first generation born in Singapore)
The family moved to Singapore in 1828, and the following children were born there. The entries are in Tan Ah Kow's own hand, and are more detailed for the sons.

7. Family of Tan Ah Kow's Cousins
Tan Ah Kow's father had two brothers, and the register includes notes on their families, as they were part of the same household in Malacca.
This section records deaths that occurred after the register was first compiled. The entries are in several hands, as different family members made additions over time. Some are in ink, some in pencil. The handwriting becomes more hurried and less legible in later entries, suggesting a change in scribe.

Tan Ah Kow's mother, Tan Seow Neo, died on 12 March 1850, at the age of seventy-two. She had been living with the family in Singapore since the move in 1828. The entry states: "She passed away peacefully in her sleep. The funeral was held at the burial ground near Bukit Timah, and was attended by many who remembered her kindness."

Tan Ah Kow's younger sister, Tan Ah Neo, died on 3 August 1862. She had never married and had lived with the family her whole life. The entry is brief: "She was taken ill with a fever and did not recover. She was buried beside her mother."

Tan Ah Kow's wife's mother, Lim Guat Neo's mother, died in Malacca in 1855. The entry notes: "News reached us by letter. The funeral was held in Malacca, and my wife could not attend as she was with child."

Infant deaths are recorded in this section as well. A child of Tan Ah Kow's cousin Tan Kim Seng, a baby girl named Tan Ah Kim, died in 1852, aged eleven months. The entry says only: "The child was buried in Malacca."

Another infant, a son of Tan Ah Kow's nephew (the eldest son of Tan Ah Lian), died in Penang in 1858. The entry was added by Tan Ah Lian herself, who wrote: "My grandson, Khoo Cheng Huat, died of a wasting illness. He was two years old. I have planted a tree at the grave."

Tan Ah Kow's brother-in-law, Lim Peng Soon's son (the brother of Lim Guat Neo), died in 1860. The entry reads: "Lim Ah Teck, brother of my wife, died in Penang where he had gone to conduct business. He was forty-one years old. He left a wife and three children."

Marginal note in pencil, in a different hand: "Uncle Lim Ah Teck's widow remarried two years later. The children were sent to a school in Penang."

9. Tan Ah Kow's Death

The family register records Tan Ah Kow's death_date as 1862-11-01. Record status: historical. This entry is in the hand of his eldest son, Tan Ah Beng, who wrote: "My father, Tan Ah Kow, died on the first day of November in the year 1862, at his house in Singapore. He was sixty-eight years old. He had been unwell for some months, but his mind remained clear until the end. He was buried at the family plot near Bukit Timah, beside his mother and sister."

The entry continues: "He was a merchant and a leader of the community. Many people came to the funeral. The street was lined with those who wished to pay their respects. The family received letters of condolence from Malacca, Penang, and as far away as Batavia."

Record status: historical. This entry is considered the authoritative record of his death in this register. No other death date for him is noted in any later volume.

Marginal note in a later hand, likely by Tan Ah Kow's grandson: "The Towkay's death was a great loss to the family and to the community. He had been active in the temple committee and in the clan association until his final illness."

10. Notes on Burials

The register includes a rough list of burial locations for family members who died in Singapore. The list is not complete, as some entries were added from memory.

- Tan Seow Neo (mother of Tan Ah Kow): Buried near Bukit Timah, in the family plot.
- Tan Ah Neo (sister of Tan Ah Kow): Buried near Bukit Timah, in the family plot.
- Tan Ah Kow: Buried near Bukit Timah, in the family plot.
- An infant daughter of Tan Ah Beng (born and died 1856): Buried in the same plot. The entry notes: "She was born in the seventh month and died in the ninth. No name was given."

The list ends with a note: "The graves were tended by the family until the land was sold in 1901. The remains were moved to a new cemetery. The exact locations of the older graves were not recorded."

11. Correspondence Noted in the Register
Record status: historical. This entry is considered the authoritative record of Tan Kim Seng's birth in this register. It has not been crossed out or amended at any point.

A further marginal note, in pencil and in a different hand, possibly that of Tan Kim Seng's own son: "My father often said he was born in the seventh month of the Chinese calendar, but the family register keeps the Western date. The two do not always agree, but the register is the record we follow."

---

12.2. Tan Ah Beng, born 1825

This entry appears earlier in the register but is repeated here in the margin of the 1830s section for reference. It is in Tan Ah Kow's hand:

"Tan Ah Beng, my firstborn son, was born on the third day of the third month in the year 1825. His mother was Lim Choo Neo. He was born in Malacca, where I was then living. He was named after my father, Tan Ah Beng, who had died the year before."

The entry is not crossed out. In the margin, a later hand has written: "Eldest son. Succeeded his father as head of the family. Died 1888."

---

12.3. Tan Kim Huat, born 1833

In ink, in Tan Ah Kow's hand:

"On the tenth day of February, in the year one thousand eight hundred and thirty-three, my wife Lim Choo Neo gave birth to a son, who was named Kim Huat. The birth occurred at our house in Singapore. The child was small but lively. He was my third son and fifth child."

In pencil, in a later hand: "Kim Huat died in Penang in 1871. He had moved there in the 1850s to manage the family's trading interests. He left no sons, only two daughters. His line ended with his daughters' marriages."

---

12.4. Tan Seow Lian, born 1835

In ink, in Tan Ah Kow's hand:

In the family register, Tan Kim Seng's birth_date is noted as 1830-07-22. Record status: historical.

"On the second day of June, in the year one thousand eight hundred and thirty-five, my wife gave birth to a daughter. She was named Seow Lian. She was my second daughter and sixth child. The birth was easy, and both mother and child were well."

In pencil, in a later hand: "Seow Lian married Lee Keng Chuan of Malacca in 1853. She had four children, all of whom survived to adulthood. She died in 1902 and was buried in Malacca. Her descendants are numerous and are recorded in a separate volume."

---

12.5. Tan Kim Chuan, born 1837

In ink, in Tan Ah Kow's hand:

"On the eighteenth day of November, in the year one thousand eight hundred and thirty-seven, my wife Lim Choo Neo gave birth to a fourth son. He was named Kim Chuan. The birth took place at our house in Singapore. This was my seventh child."

In pencil, in a later hand: "Kim Chuan never married. He was involved in the family business but was not active in public life. He died in Singapore in 1891. His estate was divided among his nephews and nieces."

---

12.6. Tan Seow Kim, born 1839

In ink, in Tan Ah Kow's hand:

"On the twenty-ninth day of March, in the year one thousand eight hundred and thirty-nine, my wife gave birth to a third daughter. She was named Seow Kim. She was my eighth child. The birth was difficult, and my wife was unwell for some weeks afterward. She recovered fully, but we had no more children after this."

In pencil, in a later hand: "Seow Kim married Tan Cheng Tiong of Singapore in 1857. They had three sons and two daughters. She died in 1910. Her husband was not related to our family despite the same surname, or so it was said at the time. The matter was looked into before the marriage and it was found that his family came from a different district in Fujian."

---

13. Note on the Numbering of Children

The register uses the terms "first son," "second son," and so on, and also counts daughters separately. The total number of children is sometimes given as eight, sometimes as nine. The explanation is that a daughter born between Tan Ah Beng and Tan Kim Seng died in infancy and was not given a name. She is not counted in the numbered list of children, but she is remembered in a separate note.
In ink, in a different hand, possibly that of Tan Ah Kow's eldest son Tan Beng Swee himself:

"On the third day of February, in the year one thousand eight hundred and sixty-three, my wife Lim Siew Neo gave birth to a daughter. She was named Jiak Guan. She was our first child. The birth took place at our house in Telok Ayer Street, where we were then living. My father was present and performed the naming ceremony."

In pencil, in the same later hand as above:

"Jiak Guan married Low Kim Pong of Singapore in 1884. They had two sons and three daughters. She died in 1929."

---

13.3. Tan Jiak Nio, born 1863

In ink, in the same hand as the previous entry:

"On the twenty-ninth day of November, in the year one thousand eight hundred and sixty-three, my wife gave birth to a second daughter. She was named Jiak Nio. She was our second child. The birth was easy, and my wife recovered quickly."

In pencil, in the later hand:

"Jiak Nio married Ong Sam Leong in 1885. They had one son and two daughters. She died in 1935 in Penang, where her husband's business was based."

---

13.4. Tan Jiak Eng, born 1866

In ink, in the same hand:

"On the second day of January, in the year one thousand eight hundred and sixty-six, my wife gave birth to a third daughter. She was named Jiak Eng. She was our third child. This child was born at the new house on River Valley Road, to which we had moved in the middle of 1865."

In pencil, in the later hand:

"Jiak Eng never married. She devoted herself to charitable work and was known for her support of the Po Leung Kuk, which assisted women and girls in need. She died in 1941."

---

13.5. Tan Jiak Chuan, born 1867

In ink, in the same hand:

In the family register, Tan Jiak Kim's birth_date is noted as 1865-05-10. Record status: historical.

"On the seventeenth day of August, in the year one thousand eight hundred and sixty-seven, my wife gave birth to a second son. He was named Jiak Chuan. He was our fourth child. The birth was difficult, and my wife was confined to bed for a month. She recovered, but the doctor advised her not to have more children."

In pencil, in the later hand:

"Jiak Chuan was educated at Raffles Institution and later joined the family firm. He died in 1901 of a fever contracted during a business trip to Sumatra. He was unmarried."

---

13.6. Tan Jiak Seng, born 1869

In ink, in the same hand:

"On the first day of March, in the year one thousand eight hundred and sixty-nine, my wife gave birth to a fifth child, a daughter. She was named Jiak Seng. This was our last child, as my wife's health was delicate after this birth."

In pencil, in the later hand:

"Jiak Seng married Lee Cheng Yan in 1890. They had three sons. She died in 1920."

---

13.7. Note on the Children of Tan Beng Swee

In ink, in the scribe's hand:

"The above five children, born between 1863 and 1869, are all the children of Tan Beng Swee, second son of Tan Ah Kow, and his wife Lim Siew Neo. The births are recorded in the order in which they occurred. The family register follows the practice of listing sons and daughters together in order of birth, rather than separately, for the generation of Tan Ah Kow's grandchildren."

In pencil, in the later hand:

"This practice was changed in later volumes, where sons and daughters are again listed separately. The reader should be aware of this difference when consulting the various volumes of the family register."

---

14. Note on the Education of the Grandchildren

In ink, in the scribe's hand:

"In the year 1872, Tan Ah Kow instructed that his grandchildren who had reached the age of six should begin their education. A schoolroom was established on the second floor of the River Valley Road house, and a teacher was engaged from Malacca. The teacher, Mr. Lim Cheng Hoe, taught reading, writing, and arithmetic in both English and Chinese. The grandchildren attended the schoolroom until they were old enough to be sent to Raffles Institution or to the Chinese free school in Amoy Street.
14.1. Note on the Schoolroom at River Valley Road

In ink, in the scribe's hand:

"The schoolroom continued in use until the year 1878, when the teacher, Mr. Lim Cheng Hoe, returned to Malacca to care for his aged mother. After his departure, the grandchildren were sent to their respective schools. The room was then used for the storage of family papers and old account books, which had previously been kept in a chest in the main hall."

In pencil, in the later hand:

"The chest referred to here was the same one that later formed the beginning of the Family Archives. It was a camphor wood chest, with a brass lock, and it stood in the corner of the schoolroom. Some of the older papers in the Archives still show the marks of having been folded to fit into that chest."

---

14.2. The Founding of the Tan Family Archives

In ink, in a formal hand, different from the scribe's hand:

"In the year one thousand eight hundred and eighty, the family being now large and its affairs numerous, it was resolved that the papers and records of the family should be gathered together and kept in a proper manner. This resolution was made by Tan Ah Kow, with the agreement of his sons and of the elders of the family. The matter was discussed at a meeting held at the River Valley Road house, on the fifteenth day of the second month of the year, and it was agreed that the papers should be kept in the room that had formerly been the schoolroom.

The family register notes the Tan Family Archives' founding_year as 1880. Record status: historical. This is the year in which the Archives were formally established, and the first entries in the catalogue of the Archives are dated in that year.

It was further resolved that a member of the family should be appointed to have charge of the papers, and that this charge should be considered an honourable one, to be held by a person of good character and careful habits. The person so appointed was to keep a catalogue of all papers, to see that they were stored in a dry and safe place, and to produce them when required by the head of the family.

The family papers had, up to that time, been kept in various places. Some were in the chest in the schoolroom, some were in the keeping of the several sons of Tan Ah Kow, and some were in the hands of the family's agent in China. It was now ordered that all these should be brought together, and that copies should be made of such papers as could not be spared from the places where they were kept.

The papers were to include the following: the family register itself, the account books of the family firm, the correspondence of Tan Ah Kow and of his father Tan Seng Poh, the title deeds of the family property, and such other documents as might be considered worthy of preservation. It was also ordered that a record should be kept of the marriages, births, and deaths of the family, and that this record should be kept in the same place as the other papers."

In pencil, in the later hand:

"The meeting referred to here was held on the fifteenth day of the second month of the Chinese calendar, which fell on the twenty-sixth day of March in the year 1880. This date is given in the margin of the original minutes, which are now in the Archives."

---

14.3. The First Archivist

In ink, in the same formal hand:

"The person appointed to have charge of the papers was Tan Ah Kow's eldest grandson, Tan Keng Swee, who was at that time twenty-two years of age. Tan Keng Swee had been educated at Raffles Institution, and had shown himself to be of a careful and orderly disposition. He had also a good knowledge of both English and Chinese, which was considered necessary for the proper keeping of the papers, many of which were in one or other of these languages.
Tan Family Register and Genealogical Notes

---

**14.4. The Second Archivist**

In ink, in the same formal hand:

"Tan Keng Swee held the charge of the papers for eleven years, from 1880 to 1891. In the latter year he was appointed to the post of chief clerk in the firm of Guthrie & Co., and it was felt that the duties of that office would not leave him sufficient leisure to attend properly to the family papers. He therefore resigned the charge, and the head of the family, Tan Ah Kow, appointed in his stead his second grandson, Tan Keng Chye, who was at that time twenty-five years of age.

Tan Keng Chye had been trained in the family firm, and had, since the age of seventeen, kept the account books of the branch in Penang. He was a man of few words, but of great accuracy in all matters of figures and dates. It was said of him that he never forgot a date once he had written it down, and that he could recall, at any moment, the particulars of any transaction that had passed through his hands. He was also, like his elder brother, well versed in both English and Chinese.

Tan Keng Chye held the charge for a shorter period than his brother. In 1895 he fell ill of a fever, and though he recovered, his health was never quite the same afterwards. He continued in the charge until 1897, when he asked to be relieved of it, on the ground that he wished to spend more time in the care of his health and in the education of his children. His request was granted, and the charge was then given to his younger brother, Tan Keng Huat."

---

**14.5. The Third Archivist**

In ink, in the same formal hand:

"Tan Keng Huat was the third son of Tan Ah Kow's eldest son, Tan Keng Chye's elder brother, Tan Keng Soon. He was at that time twenty-eight years of age. He had been educated at the Anglo-Chinese School, and had afterwards spent some years in the family's agency in Amoy, where he had gained experience in the handling of correspondence and the keeping of records.

Tan Keng Huat was of a more scholarly disposition than his brothers. He was fond of reading, and had a particular interest in the history of the family and of the Chinese community in the Straits. It was under his charge that the family papers were first arranged in the order in which they are now kept, and that the catalogue which is still in use was begun.

It was also under his charge that the present register was first begun. The earlier register, which had been kept by Tan Ah Kow himself and by his father Tan Seng Poh, had been written in a rough and uneven manner, with entries in various hands and in no fixed order. Tan Keng Huat proposed that a fair copy should be made, and that the entries should be arranged in chronological order, with such notes and annotations as might be necessary. This proposal was approved by the head of the family, and the work was begun in the year 1898.

The work was not completed until the year 1901, and it was done in the following manner. The old register was first read through, and the entries were copied out, in order, into a new book. Where the meaning of an entry was doubtful, or where two entries appeared to be in conflict with one another, the matter was referred to the older members of the family, and their recollection was taken as authority. Where the old register was silent, no attempt was made to supply the deficiency, except in those cases where the fact was well known and could be verified from other papers.

The fair copy was made in the hand of Tan Keng Huat himself, who was a good calligrapher in both languages. The entries in English were written in a clear and regular hand, and the entries in Chinese were written in the style known as kai-shu, or regular script. The pages were numbered, and the date of each entry was written in the margin, in the Gregorian calendar, with the Chinese date added in brackets where it was known."
Tan Family Register and Genealogical Notes

Continuation of the fair copy begun 1898, completed 1901, in the hand of Tan Keng Huat, with later entries by various members of the family. The register is kept in the family house at 12 Nankin Street, Singapore. Pages 45–52.

Page 45

1902, 14 March. — Tan Boon Leong, second son of Tan Keng Huat and his wife Lim Chwee Neo, was born at the family house in Nankin Street. The birth was recorded by the attending physician, Dr. J. C. Brown, and entered into the register by the father. The child was named Boon Leong, and his Chinese name is 陳文良 (Tan Boon Leong). He was the first of the children of Tan Keng Huat to be born after the completion of the fair copy of this register.

1904, 2 September. — Tan Boon Leong died of fever, aged two years and five months. He was buried at the Tan family plot at Bukit Brown, and a small stone was placed over the grave. The entry of his birth remains as first written, and this entry of his death is added in the margin by his father, who wrote: "A bright child, taken too soon."

1905, 21 January. — Tan Keng Huat's wife, Lim Chwee Neo, gave birth to a daughter, named Tan Geok Eng (陳玉英). The birth was noted in the margin of the register by Tan Keng Huat, who was at that time away in Penang on family business. The entry is in pencil, and was later overwritten in ink by Tan Keng Huat's younger brother, Tan Keng Seng, who added the date and the name of the child.

1907, 3 July. — Tan Geok Eng died of measles, aged two years and five months. She was buried beside her brother Boon Leong at Bukit Brown. The entry of her birth was not altered, but a note was added in the margin by Tan Keng Huat: "Our second child, Geok Eng, died 3 July 1907, of measles. She was a quiet child, and we miss her."

1908, 12 November. — Tan Keng Huat's third child, a son, was born. He was named Tan Boon Teck (陳文德). The birth was recorded in the register by Tan Keng Huat himself, who wrote: "A son, born this day, at half past six in the morning. His mother is well. We have named him Boon Teck, and we pray that he may live to grow up."

1910, 8 May. — Tan Keng Huat's fourth child, a daughter, was born. She was named Tan Geok Hoon (陳玉雲). The birth was recorded by Tan Keng Huat, who added: "A fine girl, and her mother says she looks like her own mother. We have named her Geok Hoon."

---

Page 46

1912, 17 February. — Tan Keng Huat's fifth child, a son, was born. He was named Tan Boon Chye (陳文才). The birth was recorded in the register by Tan Keng Huat, who wrote: "A third son. His mother is well, and the child is strong. We have named him Boon Chye."

1914, 6 October. — Tan Keng Huat's sixth child, a daughter, was born. She was named Tan Geok Kim (陳玉金). The birth was recorded by Tan Keng Huat, who added: "A fourth daughter. Her mother is well, and the child is healthy. We have named her Geok Kim."

1916, 22 April. — Tan Keng Huat's seventh child, a son, was born. He was named Tan Boon Seng (陳文成). The birth was recorded by Tan Keng Huat, who wrote: "A fourth son. His mother is well. We have named him Boon Seng."

1918, 9 December. — Tan Keng Huat's wife, Lim Chwee Neo, died of influenza, which was then sweeping through the town. She was buried at Bukit Brown, beside her two children who had died in infancy. Tan Keng Huat wrote in the register: "My dear wife, Lim Chwee Neo, died this day of the influenza. She was a good wife and a good mother, and I am left with seven children, the youngest but two years old. I do not know how I shall manage without her. The children are: Boon Teck, aged ten; Geok Hoon, aged eight; Boon Chye, aged six; Geok Kim, aged four; Boon Seng, aged two; and the two who died, Boon Leong and Geok Eng. May God have mercy on her soul."

**CORRESPONDENCE**

1. A letter from the Colonial Secretary's Office, No. 342/69, dated 28th December, 1869, regarding the proposed extension of the municipal boundary in the district of Rochore, was laid before the Commission. The letter requested the Commission's observations on the matter, and it was resolved that a sub-committee, consisting of Messrs. Cuppage and Little, be appointed to examine the question and report at the next meeting.

2. A memorial from certain ratepayers of the town, complaining of the insufficiency of the present drainage in the vicinity of Commercial Square, was read. The memorialists prayed that the Commission would take early steps to remedy the nuisance. Resolved, that the matter be referred to the Surveyor for a report.

**APPOINTMENT OF MUNICIPAL COMMISSIONER**

The Chairman informed the Commission that a vacancy had occurred in the office of Municipal Commissioner, owing to the resignation of Mr. E. J. Darby, who had left the Colony. The Chairman stated that, under the provisions of the Municipal Ordinance, it was incumbent upon the Commission to fill the vacancy by the election of a fit and proper person from among the ratepayers.

The Chairman then proposed that Tan Kim Seng, Esq., a gentleman of considerable mercantile standing and one of the largest ratepayers in the town, be appointed to the vacant office. The Chairman spoke in high terms of Mr. Tan's public spirit and his liberal contributions to charitable institutions, and expressed his belief that the appointment would be acceptable to all classes of the community.

Mr. Read seconded the motion, and it was carried unanimously.

**Resolution No. 91 — Resolved**, that Tan Kim Seng, Esq., be and is hereby appointed a Municipal Commissioner of the town of Singapore, to fill the vacancy occasioned by the resignation of Mr. E. J. Darby, and that the appointment take effect from the 1st day of January, 1870, being the date upon which the said Mr. Darby's resignation took effect.

The Secretary was directed to communicate the resolution to Mr. Tan, and to request his attendance at the next meeting.

The municipal commission minutes show Tan Kim Seng's municipal_commissioner_start as 1870-01-01. Record status: historical.

*(Handwritten note in the margin, in the Chairman's hand: "Mr. Tan has signified his acceptance verbally to me. He will attend the 18th.")*

**MUNICIPAL OFFICE — CLERK'S SALARY**

The Commission proceeded to consider the question of the salary of the Clerk to the Municipal Office, Mr. J. W. Dalziel, who had been employed in a temporary capacity since the retirement of Mr. F. S. Kemble in November last.

Mr. Little moved that Mr. Dalziel's salary be fixed at the rate of $100 per month, with effect from the 1st January, 1870, and that the appointment be confirmed. Mr. George seconded the motion.

An amendment was moved by Mr. Cuppage, that the salary be fixed at $90 per month, pending a further trial of the Clerk's abilities. The amendment was put to the vote and lost, the votes being 2 for the amendment and 4 against.

The original motion was then put and carried.

**Resolution No. 92 — Resolved**, that the appointment of Mr. J. W. Dalziel as Clerk to the Municipal Office be, and the same is hereby, confirmed, and that his salary be fixed at the rate of One Hundred Dollars ($100) per month, with effect from the 1st day of January, 1870.

**REPORT OF THE SURVEYOR — CONDITION OF THE ROADS**

The Surveyor's monthly report, for the month of December, 1869, was received and considered. The report drew attention to the very bad condition of the road leading from Kampong Glam to the Serangoon Road, which had been much cut up by the heavy traffic of bullock carts. The Surveyor estimated the cost of repairs at $1,200, and recommended that the work be put in hand without delay.
The petition was referred to the Surveyor for report, but the Chairman observed that, as Mr. Verity had just resigned, the Commission might consider it advisable to await the appointment of his successor before calling for any report upon the subject. After some discussion, it was agreed that the petition should lie on the table until the new Surveyor was appointed.

**TAN KIM SENG — APPOINTMENT TO THE COMMISSION**

The Chairman informed the Commission that he had received a letter from the Colonial Secretary, enclosing a despatch from His Excellency the Governor, notifying that Tan Kim Seng had been appointed a member of the Municipal Commission in the room of Mr. E. J. Darby, whose resignation had been accepted, and that the appointment took effect from the 1st day of January, 1870.

Mr. Tan Kim Seng, who was present, thanked the Commission for the honour that had been done him, and said that he would endeavour to discharge the duties of the office to the best of his ability. The Chairman said that he was sure the Commission would welcome Mr. Tan, whose knowledge of the town and of the wants of the native population would be of great use in their deliberations.

**CORRESPONDENCE**

Letters were read from the following persons and bodies:

1. From the Secretary of the Tanjong Pagar Dock Company, drawing the attention of the Commission to the bad state of the road leading from the town to the docks, and suggesting that the Commission should undertake the necessary repairs.

2. From Mr. A. L. Johnston, complaining of the obstruction caused by the piles of timber and firewood deposited upon the five-foot way in Boat Quay, and requesting that the Commission would take steps to have the nuisance abated.

3. From the Assistant Resident of Province Wellesley, enquiring whether the Commission had any objection to the erection of a new jetty at the mouth of the Krian River.

4. From the Secretary of the Singapore Recreation Club, requesting permission to erect a small pavilion upon the Esplanade, near the sea wall.

The several letters were ordered to be referred to the Surveyor for report, with the exception of the letter from the Tanjong Pagar Dock Company, which was ordered to be referred to a special committee, consisting of Mr. Little and Mr. George, to enquire into the matter and report to the Commission.

**REPORT OF THE FINANCE COMMITTEE**

The Finance Committee reported that they had examined the accounts for the month of December, 1869, and that they had found the same to be correct. The receipts for the month had amounted to $4,872.35, and the expenditure to $3,916.20, leaving a balance in hand of $956.15.

The report was received and adopted.

**APPOINTMENT OF A CLERK TO THE MUNICIPAL OFFICE**

The Chairman reported that, in accordance with the resolution of the last meeting, Mr. J. W. Dalziel had been appointed Clerk to the Municipal Office, at a salary of $100 per month, with effect from the 1st day of January, 1870. Mr. Dalziel had entered upon his duties on the 3rd instant, and the Chairman was glad to report that his conduct had been satisfactory.

**MUNICIPAL COMMISSION — APPOINTMENT OF TAN KIM SENG**

The municipal commission minutes record Tan Kim Seng's municipal_commissioner_end as 1879-12-31. Record status: historical.

*(Handwritten note in the margin, in the Chairman's hand: "Mr. Tan's term of office will expire at the end of 1879. I have spoken to him, and he has signified his intention of not seeking re-appointment. We shall have to look for a successor in due course.")*

**REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON THE STATE OF THE ROADS**

The Committee appointed at the last meeting to enquire into the state of the roads in the neighbourhood of the town, and to report upon the best means of improving the same, presented their report. The Committee had examined the roads leading to Kampong Glam, to Rochore, and to the Serangoon Road, and they reported that the roads were generally in a very defective state, and that the traffic of heavy bullock carts had cut them up very badly.
**MINUTES OF THE SINGAPORE MUNICIPAL COMMISSION**

**Meeting held at the Municipal Office on Monday, the 21st day of February, 1870, at 11 o'clock a.m.**

**Present:**

His Honour the Chairman, Mr. W. H. Read
Mr. T. Scott
Mr. A. L. Johnston
Mr. J. Guthrie
Mr. C. P. Keppel
Mr. H. M. Simons
Mr. Tan Kim Seng
Mr. R. Little
Mr. W. H. M. Robins

The minutes of the last meeting were read and confirmed.

**LETTERS READ**

Letters were read from the following persons, and the same were ordered to be referred to the Surveyor for report and recommendation, with the exception of the letter from the Tanjong Pagar Dock Company, which was ordered to be referred to a special committee, consisting of Mr. Little and Mr. George, to enquire into the matter and report to the Commission.

1. From Messrs. Guthrie & Co., dated 14th instant, applying for permission to erect a godown on the reclaimed ground at Teluk Ayer, on the same terms as those granted to other applicants.
2. From Mr. H. C. C. Chan, dated 15th instant, complaining of the obstruction caused by the accumulation of night-soil in the drain running past his premises in North Bridge Road.
3. From the Secretary of the Tanjong Pagar Dock Company, dated 16th instant, requesting the sanction of the Commission to the laying of a water-main across the road leading to their new dock, and offering to defray the cost of the same, subject to the approval of the Engineer.
4. From Mr. C. H. W. Read, dated 17th instant, requesting that the Commission would take into consideration the propriety of establishing a fire-brigade in the town, and offering to subscribe the sum of $100 towards the expense of the same.
5. From the Registrar of the Supreme Court, dated 18th instant, transmitting a copy of the order of the Court directing the Commission to pay to the Sheriff the sum of $250, being the amount of costs awarded against the Commission in the matter of the petition of Mr. A. B. Smith.

**REPORT OF THE SURVEYOR ON THE STATE OF THE STREET LAMPS**

The Surveyor reported that he had, in accordance with the instructions of the Commission, caused a survey to be made of all the street lamps in the town, and that he had found the same to be in a very defective state. Many of the lamps were broken, and the glass was in many cases missing. The Surveyor was of opinion that the lamps should be repaired, and that a new system of lighting should be adopted. He recommended that the Commission should call for tenders for the supply of oil and for the cleaning and trimming of the lamps, and that the same should be let by contract.

The Chairman said that he had received a communication from the Municipal Engineer, Mr. J. W. Dalziel, on the subject of the street lamps, and he read the same to the Commission. The Engineer was of opinion that the present system of lighting was very defective, and that it would be better to adopt the system of gas-lighting, which had been introduced with great success in other towns in the East. He estimated the cost of laying the gas-pipes at $10,000, and the annual cost of lighting at $4,000. The Chairman said that he had also received a letter from Mr. Tan Kim Seng on the same subject, and he read the same to the Commission.

Mr. Tan Kim Seng said that he had been in communication with a firm in London, and that he had received from them a specimen of a new kind of lamp, which he believed would give a much better light than the lamps now in use, and at a much less cost. He would be happy to place the same at the disposal of the Commission.

After some discussion, it was resolved, on the motion of Mr. Scott, seconded by Mr. Johnston, that the Surveyor be instructed to call for tenders for the supply of oil and for the cleaning and trimming of the lamps, for a period of one year, and that the same be let by contract, and that the Engineer be instructed to report on the advisability of adopting the system of gas-lighting.

ARRIVALS.

Jan 1. S.S. Malacca, from Penang, with cargo and passengers. Agent: Messrs. Guthrie & Co.

Jan 1. S.S. Rajah, from Palembang, with a cargo of pepper and rattans. Agent: Messrs. Tan & Co.

Jan 1. S.S. Bintang, for Hongkong, with cargo and passengers. Among the passengers was Mr. A. L. Johnston, who proceeds to Japan for the recovery of his health.
Jan 1. S.S. Kin Lee, for Bangkok, with a general cargo. Agent: Messrs. Paterson, Simons & Co.
Jan 1. Barque Flora Macdonald, for London, with a cargo of tin, pepper, and sago. Agent: Messrs. Boustead & Co.

OVERLAND MAIL.

The French mail steamer arrived this morning with European papers to the 10th ult. The principal items of news are summarised elsewhere. It is reported that the disturbances in Madagascar have assumed a more serious aspect, and that the French Government have decided to despatch a further expeditionary force. The Chinese indemnity question is still unsettled, and the Powers are said to be awaiting a reply from Pekin. The Home News is of a quiet character, the chief topic of interest being the approaching meeting of Parliament.

LOCAL AND GENERAL.

The Singapore Free Press reports Tan Jiak Kim's political_activist_start as 1895-01-01. Record status: historical.

OPENING OF THE NEW YEAR. — The new year was ushered in with the usual demonstrations. The firing of crackers and the beating of gongs was kept up with great vigour throughout the night, and the Chinese portion of the town presented a most animated appearance. The streets were thronged with holiday-makers, and the various places of amusement were well attended. The weather was fine, and the thermometer registered 83 deg. in the shade at noon.

THE CHINESE NEW YEAR. — The Chinese New Year falls on the 25th instant. The usual holidays will be observed by the mercantile community, and it is expected that business will be almost entirely suspended for three days. The various kongsis are making preparations for the annual festivities.

MUNICIPAL MATTERS. — The Municipal Commissioners met on Monday last, at the Town Hall. The Acting President, Mr. J. P. Joaquim, occupied the chair. There was a good attendance of members. The principal business transacted was the consideration of the report of the Streets and Bridges Committee, recommending the repair of the causeway across the Rochor River, and the construction of a new drain in North Bridge Road. The report was adopted. A letter was read from the Secretary of State for the Colonies regarding the proposed new waterworks, and the matter was referred to a special committee for further enquiry. The question of the scavenging of the town was again brought forward, and it was decided that the present system be continued for another year.

THE SUPREME COURT. — The sittings of the Supreme Court, which were adjourned for the Christmas holidays, will be resumed on Monday next, the 7th instant, before His Honour Sir W. H. Cox. The civil side is expected to be heavy, there being a large number of cases on the list. Several important actions arising out of the failure of the Leong Bee firm are included.

POLICE REPORT. — A Chinaman named Ah Keng was charged at the Police Court on Tuesday, before Mr. A. C. B. Mowbray, with having stolen a quantity of cloth from the premises of Messrs. A. L. Johnston & Co. The accused was arrested by Sergeant No. 45, who found the property in his possession. He was committed for trial.
Jan 2. Brig "Cora," 180 tons, W. Brown, master, from Calcutta, in ballast. Consignees, Messrs. A. L. Johnston & Co.

Jan 2. Ship "Hindustan," 650 tons, R. Jones, master, from London, with a valuable cargo of piece goods, iron, and sundries. Consignees, Messrs. Maclaine, Fraser & Co.

CLEARANCES.

Dec 30. Ship "Anna," 400 tons, T. Scott, master, for Canton, with a cargo of opium, piece goods, and sundries.

Jan 2. Schooner "Rover," 70 tons, J. Thomson, master, for Malacca, with a cargo of sugar and coffee.

The "Hindustan" brings files of London papers to the 20th November. They contain no news of a very stirring nature. The accounts from the continent are, upon the whole, of a pacific tendency.

BIRTHS, MARRIAGES, & DEATHS.

MARRIED.—At St. Andrew's Church, on the 30th ult., by the Rev. F. J. Thomas, Mr. William C. Scott, of the firm of Messrs. Scott & Co., to Mary, eldest daughter of the late Mr. Alexander Ross.

DEATHS.—On the 31st ult., at his residence in the Campong, Mr. John Macdonald, aged 57, much regretted by a large circle of friends. The funeral will leave his late residence at 4 o'clock this afternoon.

On the 1st inst., at her residence in High Street, Mrs. Sarah Ann Bates, relict of the late Mr. Henry Bates, aged 63.

On the 2d inst., at the residence of his son, Mr. James Smith, of the firm of Messrs. Smith, Elder & Co., of this town, Mr. Thomas Smith, aged 81, a resident of this settlement for upwards of twenty years. The funeral will leave the residence of his son, in the Campong, at 5 o'clock this afternoon.

COMMERCIAL.

The Singapore Free Press records its publication_date as 1835-08-01. Record status: historical.

The market for opium has been rather dull during the week, prices having slightly declined. The demand for piece goods is moderate, but the supply is abundant. The arrivals from Calcutta and London during the week have been considerable, and the market is likely to be well supplied for some time.

The following are the latest quotations:—

Opium, Benares, per chest, $780 to $800.
Opium, Patna, per chest, $750 to $770.
Sugar, No. 1, per pecul, $4.50 to $4.75.
Coffee, per pecul, $12 to $13.
Pepper, per pecul, $12 to $13.

GOVERNMENT NOTICE.

It is hereby notified for general information, that the Honourable the Resident Councillor will be at home on Wednesday next, the 7th instant, from 10 o'clock A.M. to 2 o'clock P.M., for the purpose of transacting business with the inhabitants of the settlement.

By order of the Resident Councillor,
J. B. WESTERN,
Acting Secretary to Government.

Singapore, 2d January, 1835.

POLICE REPORT.

A Chinese woman, named Chong Neo, was charged at the Police Court on Thursday, before Mr. A. C. B. Mowbray, with having stolen a gold ring from the person of another woman. The complainant stated that the prisoner had been lodging in her house, and that the ring was missing shortly after the prisoner had left. The prisoner was committed for trial, bail being refused.

A sailor, named James Wilson, was fined $5 for being drunk and disorderly in the streets on New Year's Day.

THE NEW CHURCH.

We have been favoured with a copy of the report of the Committee appointed to select a site for the new church, which will be submitted to the general meeting on Monday next. The Committee state that they have examined several pieces of ground, and that they have come to the conclusion that the most eligible spot is one on Government Hill, near the flagstaff. The ground is, we believe, the property of Government, and it is hoped that it will be granted for the purpose. The Committee also recommend that a portion of the ground be reserved for a parsonage house. We shall give the report in full in our next.
SINGAPORE FREE PRESS.

SATURDAY, 10TH JANUARY, 1835.

We have received files from Calcutta to the 20th ultimo, and from Madras to the 17th ultimo. The intelligence from Europe is to the 18th November. The accounts from the upper provinces of India are of a satisfactory nature. The rains have been abundant, and the harvest is expected to be good. The health of the troops is reported to be excellent.

The Honourable the Court of Directors have appointed Captain William Farquhar to be Governor of Prince of Wales Island, Singapore, and Malacca, in the room of Mr. Kenneth Murchison, who retires from the service. This appointment gives general satisfaction. Captain Farquhar is well known to the mercantile community of these settlements, and his long experience in the Straits will, we doubt not, render his administration highly beneficial to the public interests.

We understand that the Honourable the Resident Councillor has received a communication from the Government of India, relative to the formation of a new settlement on the island of Labuan. The particulars have not transpired; but it is reported that a party of surveyors has already been despatched to examine the coast. We shall probably be able to lay further particulars before our readers in an early number.

SHIPPING INTELLIGENCE.

ARRIVALS.

Jan. 3. Ship "Diana," from London, 110 days passage. Cargo of piece goods, iron, and sundries.
Jan. 5. Brig "Fairy," from Calcutta, with a cargo of rice, sugar, and gunnies.
Jan. 6. Barque "Cora," from Penang, with a general cargo.
Jan. 8. Schooner "Swift," from Malacca, with a small cargo of fruit and vegetables.

DEPARTURES.

Jan. 5. Ship "Catherine," for London, with a full cargo of pepper, coffee, and tin.
Jan. 7. Brig "Triumph," for Madras, with a cargo of piece goods and opium.
Jan. 9. Schooner "Lark," for Penang, in ballast.

The ship "Diana" brings files of London papers to the 18th November. The accounts of the British markets are favourable. Consols have advanced to 92½. The cotton market is steady. The demand for India produce in London is good, particularly for coffee and pepper.

MARKET REPORT.

The market for opium has been somewhat dull during the week, and prices have declined. Benares is now quoted at $770 to $790 per chest, and Patna at $740 to $760. The arrival of the "Diana" has brought a fresh supply, and holders are anxious to sell. The demand for piece goods is steady. Bengal and Madras piece goods are in fair request. The stock of sugar is moderate, and the price remains as quoted in our last. Coffee has advanced slightly, and is now quoted at $12.50 to $13.50 per pecul. Pepper is firm, with sales effected at $13 per pecul. Tin is in good demand, and the price has advanced to $25 per pecul. The market for sago is dull. We quote the following as the current prices:—

Opium, Benares, per chest, $770 to $790.
Opium, Patna, per chest, $740 to $760.
Sugar, No. 1, per pecul, $4.50 to $4.75.
Sugar, No. 2, per pecul, $4.25 to $4.50.
Coffee, per pecul, $12.50 to $13.50.
Pepper, per pecul, $13.
Tin, per pecul, $25.
Sago, per pecul, $3.50 to $4.

A considerable quantity of coffee has been shipped during the week for the London market, and the shippers are likely to realize a good profit.

THE NEW CHURCH.

We have been favoured with a copy of the report of the Committee appointed to select a site for the new church, which was submitted to the general meeting held on Monday last. The report was read by the Chairman, the Honourable the Resident Councillor, and it was unanimously adopted. The Committee recommend that the church be built on Government Hill, near the flagstaff, on a piece of ground which has been granted for the purpose by Government. The ground, it appears, is amply sufficient for the church, a parsonage house, and a small burial ground. The Committee also recommend that the church be built of brick, with a tower and spire, and that it be capable of accommodating not less than 500 persons. The estimate of the cost is $12,000. A subscription list has been opened at the office of the Singapore Free Press, and we understand that upwards of $4,000 has already been subscribed.

documents.title: Tan Family Register and Genealogical Notes
documents.content:
---

1. Tan Ah Kow (頭家, "Towkay" Tan)
Birth: 15 March 1810 (recorded in the hand of his father, Tan Seng Huat, on the day of the birth; the entry is in ink and remains the authoritative record for all later family histories).

The entry reads: "On this fifteenth day of the third month, in the year of our Lord eighteen hundred and ten, was born to me, Tan Seng Huat, and my wife Lim Neo, a son. He is the firstborn. We name him Ah Kow. May he grow strong and bring honour to the family. This I write with my own hand, at Malacca."

Marginal note, added by Tan Ah Kow's eldest grandson, Tan Boon Keng, in 1895: "This is the date of the Towkay's birth. All other dates given for him in later papers are mistaken. He was born in Malacca, not in Penang as some say. He came to Singapore in 1828."

A second marginal note, in pencil, by an unknown hand, likely in the 1930s: "The old Towkay's birth date is sometimes given as 1810-03-15. This is the correct one, as per this register."

2. Tan Seng Huat (father of Tan Ah Kow)
Birth: circa 1775, in Malacca. The exact day is not recorded. He was the son of Tan Cheng Kee, a trader in spices and cloth.
Death: 12 June 1835, at Malacca. The entry is in the hand of Tan Ah Kow, who was present at the deathbed. The cause is noted as "a long illness of the chest."

3. Lim Neo (mother of Tan Ah Kow, née Lim)
Birth: circa 1778, in Malacca. Her family were farmers in the hinterland.
Death: 3 January 1840, at Singapore, in the house of her son. The entry notes: "She had come to live with her son in the new settlement, and was happy to see her grandchildren. She died in her sleep, at the age of about sixty-two."

In the family register, Tan Ah Kow's birth_date is noted as 1810-03-15. Record status: historical.

4. Tan Ah Kow's Siblings
The register lists the following brothers and sisters, all born in Malacca. The dates for the younger children are less precise, as they were recorded from memory by the mother.

- Tan Ah Lian (sister), born circa 1812. Married a trader from Penang, one Khoo Cheng Teik, in 1830. She moved to Penang and had three children. The register notes: "She is well, and writes to us sometimes." No death date is recorded in this volume.
- Tan Ah Chye (brother), born circa 1814. Died in infancy, in 1815, of fever. The entry is terse: "The child did not live to see his second year."
- Tan Ah Seng (brother), born 1817, on a date not specified. He became a planter in Province Wellesley. Married in 1843 to a woman named Goh Kim Neo. The register records the marriage but gives no further details. He is mentioned in later entries as a correspondent.
- Tan Ah Neo (sister), born circa 1820. She remained unmarried and lived with the family until her death in 1862, which is recorded in a later volume.

5. Notes on Tan Ah Kow's Marriage
Tan Ah Kow married Lim Guat Neo, daughter of Lim Peng Soon, a Malacca merchant, in 1832. The entry is in the hand of the bride's father, who wrote: "On the twentieth day of the sixth month, I gave my daughter to Tan Ah Kow, a young man of good character and prospects. The ceremony was held at my house in Malacca. May they be blessed with many sons."

Marginal note by Tan Ah Kow's grandson: "The Towkay's wife was known as 'Bibik Guat'. She was a strong woman, and managed the household while he built his business."

6. Tan Ah Kow's Children (first generation born in Singapore)
The family moved to Singapore in 1828, and the following children were born there. The entries are in Tan Ah Kow's own hand, and are more detailed for the sons.

7. Family of Tan Ah Kow's Cousins
Tan Ah Kow's father had two brothers, and the register includes notes on their families, as they were part of the same household in Malacca.

documents.title: Tan Family Register and Genealogical Notes
documents.content:
This section records deaths that occurred after the register was first compiled. The entries are in several hands, as different family members made additions over time. Some are in ink, some in pencil. The handwriting becomes more hurried and less legible in later entries, suggesting a change in scribe.

Tan Ah Kow's mother, Tan Seow Neo, died on 12 March 1850, at the age of seventy-two. She had been living with the family in Singapore since the move in 1828. The entry states: "She passed away peacefully in her sleep. The funeral was held at the burial ground near Bukit Timah, and was attended by many who remembered her kindness."

Tan Ah Kow's younger sister, Tan Ah Neo, died on 3 August 1862. She had never married and had lived with the family her whole life. The entry is brief: "She was taken ill with a fever and did not recover. She was buried beside her mother."

Tan Ah Kow's wife's mother, Lim Guat Neo's mother, died in Malacca in 1855. The entry notes: "News reached us by letter. The funeral was held in Malacca, and my wife could not attend as she was with child."

Infant deaths are recorded in this section as well. A child of Tan Ah Kow's cousin Tan Kim Seng, a baby girl named Tan Ah Kim, died in 1852, aged eleven months. The entry says only: "The child was buried in Malacca."

Another infant, a son of Tan Ah Kow's nephew (the eldest son of Tan Ah Lian), died in Penang in 1858. The entry was added by Tan Ah Lian herself, who wrote: "My grandson, Khoo Cheng Huat, died of a wasting illness. He was two years old. I have planted a tree at the grave."

Tan Ah Kow's brother-in-law, Lim Peng Soon's son (the brother of Lim Guat Neo), died in 1860. The entry reads: "Lim Ah Teck, brother of my wife, died in Penang where he had gone to conduct business. He was forty-one years old. He left a wife and three children."

Marginal note in pencil, in a different hand: "Uncle Lim Ah Teck's widow remarried two years later. The children were sent to a school in Penang."

9. Tan Ah Kow's Death

The family register records Tan Ah Kow's death_date as 1862-11-01. Record status: historical. This entry is in the hand of his eldest son, Tan Ah Beng, who wrote: "My father, Tan Ah Kow, died on the first day of November in the year 1862, at his house in Singapore. He was sixty-eight years old. He had been unwell for some months, but his mind remained clear until the end. He was buried at the family plot near Bukit Timah, beside his mother and sister."

The entry continues: "He was a merchant and a leader of the community. Many people came to the funeral. The street was lined with those who wished to pay their respects. The family received letters of condolence from Malacca, Penang, and as far away as Batavia."

Record status: historical. This entry is considered the authoritative record of his death in this register. No other death date for him is noted in any later volume.

Marginal note in a later hand, likely by Tan Ah Kow's grandson: "The Towkay's death was a great loss to the family and to the community. He had been active in the temple committee and in the clan association until his final illness."

10. Notes on Burials

The register includes a rough list of burial locations for family members who died in Singapore. The list is not complete, as some entries were added from memory.

- Tan Seow Neo (mother of Tan Ah Kow): Buried near Bukit Timah, in the family plot.
- Tan Ah Neo (sister of Tan Ah Kow): Buried near Bukit Timah, in the family plot.
- Tan Ah Kow: Buried near Bukit Timah, in the family plot.
- An infant daughter of Tan Ah Beng (born and died 1856): Buried in the same plot. The entry notes: "She was born in the seventh month and died in the ninth. No name was given."

The list ends with a note: "The graves were tended by the family until the land was sold in 1901. The remains were moved to a new cemetery. The exact locations of the older graves were not recorded."

11. Correspondence Noted in the Register
